title: Amazon's $69 Billion Hidden Tax: The $100 Unit Economics Breakdown

scenes.title: Where $100 of Amazon Sales Actually Goes
scenes.footnote: Illustrative model · typical third-party apparel seller · per $100 of sales · Sources: Marketplace Pulse; Amazon 2026 fee schedule

steps.label: Customer Sales
steps.sub: $100 of sales. Who actually keeps it?
steps.cue: Every time you spend one hundred dollars
steps.narration: Every time you spend one hundred dollars with a seller on Amazon... about fifty-two of those dollars never reach the seller. Not the brand. Not the factory. Amazon. Last year, a single line in Amazon's annual report — advertising — brought in sixty-eight point six billion dollars. That's roughly one hundred and eighty-eight million dollars... every single day. In the next nine minutes, we'll follow one hundred dollars of sales — dollar by dollar — through every fee, every auction, and every return. And by the end, you'll see why the U.S. government has taken Amazon to court over it — twice... and why, according to the FTC, you may be paying this tax even if you never shop on Amazon at all.

steps.label: Product & Freight
steps.sub: Manufacturing, ocean freight and import duties — paid months before anything sells.
steps.cue: Here's a typical apparel seller on Amazon
steps.narration: Here's a typical apparel seller on Amazon — modeled from Marketplace Pulse data and Amazon's own fee schedule — per hundred dollars in sales. First, the product itself. Manufacturing, ocean freight, and import duties. Twenty-eight dollars — paid months before anything sells.

steps.label: Referral Fee (17%)
steps.sub: Amazon's first cut: a 17% referral fee on apparel over $20.
steps.cue: The moment a customer clicks "Buy Now"...
steps.narration: The moment a customer clicks "Buy Now"... Amazon takes its first cut. A seventeen percent referral fee on clothing. Seventeen dollars.

steps.label: FBA, Storage & Surcharges
steps.sub: Picking, packing, shipping, storage — plus a 3.5% surcharge since April 2026.
steps.cue: Next, Fulfillment by Amazon. Picking, packing, shipping,
steps.narration: Next, Fulfillment by Amazon. Picking, packing, shipping, storage... plus a new surcharge added this April. About twenty dollars.

steps.label: Sponsored Ads
steps.sub: The line shoppers never see: about $15 of every $100 goes to sponsored listings.
steps.cue: Then, the line shoppers never see. Advertising.
steps.narration: Then, the line shoppers never see. Advertising. Just to show up where buyers look, a typical seller spends around fifteen dollars on sponsored listings.

steps.label: Returns & Write-offs
steps.sub: Refunds, return fees and inventory that can't be resold.
steps.cue: Returns and write-offs take another ten.
steps.narration: Returns and write-offs take another ten.

steps.label: Seller Keeps
steps.sub: The seller keeps $10. Amazon collects $52 — more than five times as much.

boxes.title: Seller keeps
boxes.sub: after product, fees, ads and returns

steps.cue: The final split? The seller — who
steps.narration: The final split? The seller — who designed the product, paid the factory, and carried all the risk — keeps about ten dollars. Amazon — without owning a single thread — collects about fifty-two. More than five times what the seller keeps. And that fifteen-dollar ad line? That's the one that quietly became a sixty-eight-billion-dollar business.

scenes.title: How a Digital Shelf Became an Ad Auction
scenes.footnote: Sources: Amazon FY2025 Form 10-K; WAN-IFRA 2025; Jungle Scout 2024; Constructor 2025; FTC v. Amazon (2026, allegations); Marketplace Pulse

layers.name: Amazon search (56–63% of US shoppers start here)

steps.label: 1. The 10-K Line
steps.sub: More than half the revenue of every daily and weekly newspaper on Earth ($125.7B).
steps.cue: How did an online bookstore become a
steps.narration: How did an online bookstore become a toll collector? The answer is buried in Amazon's SEC Form ten-K, under a line called "advertising services." In 2025, it brought in sixty-eight point six billion dollars — up twenty-two percent in a single year. For perspective... that's more than half the combined revenue of every daily and weekly newspaper on Earth. Not all of it comes from sellers — Prime Video and Twitch ads count too — but sponsored search listings are widely estimated to be the biggest piece.

steps.label: 2. Demand Lock-In
steps.sub: Share of US online shoppers who start product searches on Amazon (Jungle Scout 2024 · Constructor 2025).
steps.cue: Here's how it works. Depending on the
steps.narration: Here's how it works. Depending on the survey, between half and two-thirds of American online shoppers now start their product searches directly on Amazon. And once the buyers are all in one room... whoever controls the shelf controls the business.

steps.label: 3. The Pay-to-Play Shelf
steps.sub: Every slot is a seller bidding per click against other sellers for the same customer.
steps.broll: Creator's own phone screen recording of an Amazon search
steps.cue: So Amazon turned the shelf into an
steps.narration: So Amazon turned the shelf into an auction. Try it yourself: search for almost anything on your phone... and count the "Sponsored" results before the first one that isn't. Every slot is a seller bidding, per click, against other sellers.

steps.label: 4. The Hidden Surcharge (Alleged)
steps.sub: FTC + 22 states allege a secret surcharge on top of auction prices since 2019: $20B+ overcharged.

evidence.doc: FTC et al. v. Amazon.com, Inc. (W.D. Wash.), filed Aug. 31, 2026
evidence.quote: Alleged: up to 50% above auction results on ordinary days, up to 250% on peak days

steps.cue: And according to a new lawsuit, even
steps.narration: And according to a new lawsuit, even the auction may not be what it seems. In August 2026, the FTC and twenty-two states sued Amazon, alleging that since 2019 it secretly added a surcharge on top of auction prices. Documents unsealed in November allege prices up to fifty percent above the auction result on ordinary days... and up to two hundred and fifty percent on days like Prime Day. The FTC puts the total overcharge at more than twenty billion dollars. Amazon calls the suit misguided, and says it never charges more than an advertiser's maximum bid.

steps.label: 5. The Bottleneck
steps.sub: Fees + ads ≈ 52% of seller sales (Marketplace Pulse, 2022 average: 51.8%).
steps.cue: For sellers, it's a prisoner's dilemma: bid
steps.narration: For sellers, it's a prisoner's dilemma: bid away your margin... or disappear. So why don't they just charge less everywhere else? Because if they try... a bot is watching.

scenes.title: The Price Floor & Project Nessie
scenes.footnote: FTC claims are allegations; Amazon denies wrongdoing. Buy Box share is an industry estimate not confirmed by Amazon.

steps.label: 1. The Price-Parity Trap
steps.sub: What happens when a seller charges less off Amazon?

evidence.doc: FTC et al. v. Amazon.com, Inc., No. 2:23-cv-01495 (W.D. Wash.)

steps.cue: In 2023, the Federal Trade Commission and
steps.narration: In 2023, the Federal Trade Commission and a group of states sued Amazon for illegally maintaining a monopoly. The complaint describes what happens when a seller tries to undercut Amazon. Say you sell a dress for one hundred dollars on Amazon... and eighty-five on your own Shopify store, where your fees are lower.

steps.label: 2. The Buy Box
steps.sub: FTC: discounting sellers can become "effectively invisible."

evidence.doc: FTC et al. v. Amazon.com, Inc., No. 2:23-cv-01495 (W.D. Wash.), Dkt. 1, p. 9

steps.cue: According to the FTC, Amazon's algorithms scan
steps.narration: According to the FTC, Amazon's algorithms scan the internet for lower prices. If they find one, your offer can lose the Buy Box — that yellow "Add to Cart" button. Industry estimates — never confirmed by Amazon — say more than eighty percent of sales go through it. The complaint goes further. It says Amazon can bury discounting sellers so far down in search results that they become — quote — "effectively invisible." So sellers do the rational thing. In the FTC's words, they use their inflated Amazon prices as "a price floor everywhere else"... which means, if the government is right, you pay the Amazon tax even at other stores.

steps.label: 3. Project Nessie
steps.sub: FTC alleges $1B+ in extra profit. Amazon: the FTC "grossly mischaracterizes" the tool.

evidence.quote: Alleged: more than $1 billion in excess profit

steps.cue: Then there's Project Nessie — an algorithm
steps.narration: Then there's Project Nessie — an algorithm the FTC says predicted when competitors would match Amazon's price increases... so Amazon could raise prices and watch rivals follow. The agency alleges it generated more than one billion dollars in extra profit. Amazon says the FTC "grossly mischaracterizes" the tool — and that it was scrapped because it didn't work as intended. More broadly, Amazon says the lawsuit is wrong on the facts and the law. But there's one cost we haven't counted yet... the one that arrives after the sale is over.

scenes.title: The True Cost of One "Free" $100 Return
scenes.footnote: One worn $100 dress · 17% referral fee · ≈ values vary by size and weight · Sources: NRF 2025; Appriss Retail; Amazon fee policies 2026

steps.label: Sale Reversed
steps.sub: The customer gets $100 back. The sale no longer exists.
steps.cue: Now for the cost that comes back
steps.narration: Now for the cost that comes back in a box. According to the National Retail Federation, roughly one in five online purchases gets sent back. In fashion, there's a name for one of the most common forms of abuse. Wardrobing. Buy an evening dress on Friday. Wear it to a wedding on Saturday. Return it on Monday — "didn't fit." In one industry survey, sixty percent of retail executives said they'd seen wardrobing — the most common type of return fraud on the list. For the shopper, the return is free. For the seller, here's what one worn, one-hundred-dollar dress actually costs.

steps.label: Refund Admin Fee
steps.sub: Amazon keeps 20% of the $17 referral fee (capped at $5).
steps.cue: The customer gets their hundred dollars back.
steps.narration: The customer gets their hundred dollars back. Amazon refunds most of its referral fee... but keeps a refund administration fee. Three dollars and forty cents.

steps.label: FBA Fee Not Refunded
steps.sub: The fulfillment fee Amazon charged to ship the dress is gone.
steps.cue: The fulfillment fee Amazon charged to ship
steps.narration: The fulfillment fee Amazon charged to ship the dress? Not refunded. About six dollars... gone.

steps.label: Returns Processing
steps.sub: Apparel returns processing fee (roughly $1.65–$3.89 by size).
steps.cue: Then, a returns processing fee. Around three
steps.narration: Then, a returns processing fee. Around three dollars more.

steps.label: Worn Dress Written Off
steps.sub: Makeup and perfume: it can't be sold as new.
steps.cue: And the dress itself comes back with
steps.narration: And the dress itself comes back with makeup on the collar and perfume in the fabric. It can't be sold as new. Twenty-eight dollars of inventory... written off.

steps.label: Net Loss
steps.sub: = the profit from four full-price sales at a 10% margin.

boxes.title: One wardrobed return
boxes.sub: wipes out the profit from 4 full-price sales

steps.cue: Total: a loss of about forty dollars
steps.narration: Total: a loss of about forty dollars and forty cents — on a sale that no longer exists. At a ten percent margin, that's four full-price sales... just to pay for one wardrobed dress. And even the sellers who survive returns run into a trap that has nothing to do with customers. It's about time.

scenes.title: Cash Out First, Paid Last — Fined Either Way
scenes.footnote: Sources: Amazon seller policies (delivery-date reserve, inbound placement, low-inventory-level fee); 3.5% surcharge eff. Apr 17, 2026; Marketplace Pulse 2026 Seller Index

steps.label: 1. Factory Cash Goes Out
steps.sub: Sellers pay factories long before a single unit reaches a customer.
steps.cue: Selling on Amazon starts with a bet.
steps.narration: Selling on Amazon starts with a bet. Sellers pay their factories up front — often two or three months before a single unit reaches a customer.

steps.label: 2. The Payout Reserve
steps.sub: Funds release 7 days after confirmed delivery — often 2–4 weeks from sale to bank.
steps.cue: Then, when the sale finally happens, the
steps.narration: Then, when the sale finally happens, the money still doesn't arrive. Under Amazon's current rules, seller funds generally become available seven days after the customer's confirmed delivery. Add settlement cycles on top, and many sellers wait two to four weeks to touch their own revenue.

steps.label: 3. Fees Around Inventory
steps.sub: Inbound placement fee (since 2024) + 3.5% on every fulfillment fee (April 2026).
steps.cue: Meanwhile, the fees around the inventory keep
steps.narration: Meanwhile, the fees around the inventory keep multiplying. Since 2024, Amazon has charged an inbound placement fee — essentially, a fee based on how your boxes get distributed across its warehouses. And in April 2026, it added a three-and-a-half percent surcharge on every fulfillment fee.

steps.label: 4. The Corridor
steps.sub: Aged-inventory surcharge vs. low-inventory fee. 49% of sellers call fees their #1 margin concern.
steps.cue: And then there's the corridor. Keep too
steps.narration: And then there's the corridor. Keep too much stock for too long, and you pay aged inventory surcharges. But let your stock fall below roughly twenty-eight days of supply... and you pay a low-inventory-level fee on every unit shipped. Too much costs money. Too little costs money. Amazon collects on both sides. No surprise, then, that in Marketplace Pulse's 2026 Seller Index, forty-nine percent of sellers named fees as their biggest margin concern — and forty-six percent named advertising. So... why does anyone stay?

scenes.title: The Tollbooth, Then and Now
scenes.footnote: Sources: Stripe standard pricing; Amazon 2020 shareholder letter; Marketplace Pulse; FTC v. Amazon (W.D. Wash.)

steps.label: 1. The Alternative Isn't Free
steps.rightText: Own store: card fee ≈ $3.20 + paid traffic (?)
steps.sub: 2.9% + 30¢ to process the card — but the customers still have to be bought on Google, Meta or TikTok.
steps.cue: On your own website, the payment processor
steps.narration: On your own website, the payment processor takes about three dollars on a hundred-dollar sale. Sounds like a bargain... until you realize the customers don't come with it. You have to buy them — one click at a time — on Google, Meta, or TikTok. A different auction... with the same tollbooth logic. And Amazon does deliver something real. Over two hundred million Prime members, fast delivery, and a checkout button people trust without thinking. That's what sellers are paying for.

steps.label: 2. What Changed Is the Price
steps.sub: Amazon's average cut of seller sales (Marketplace Pulse).

evidence.doc: FTC et al. v. Amazon.com, Inc., No. 2:23-cv-01495 (W.D. Wash.)

steps.cue: What's changed is the price. In 2016,
steps.narration: What's changed is the price. In 2016, Amazon's cut was about a third of a seller's revenue. By 2022, it was more than half. And in 2027, a federal judge in Seattle will start deciding whether parts of how Amazon got here broke the law. If the FTC wins, the Buy Box rules could change... and with them, prices across the internet. If Amazon wins, the tollbooth stays.

steps.label: 3. Back to the $100
steps.sub: The fortune belongs to whoever controls the last three seconds before checkout.
steps.cue: So... back to where we started. When
steps.narration: So... back to where we started. When you spend one hundred dollars with a seller on Amazon — who actually gets your money? About ten dollars goes to the business that made the product. About fifty-two goes to the company that owns the shelf. In modern commerce, the company that makes the product rarely gets rich. The fortune belongs to whoever controls the last three seconds before checkout. Every number in this video is sourced in the description.
